experiment.rationale:
Five experts with clearly ordered, well-spread validities (0.95, 0.85, 0.75, 0.65, 0.55) so that Take-The-Best's cue cascade is unambiguous. The 12 unique pairs (each repeated 8 times, ~96 trials) are chosen to create four distinct diagnostic classes:

(1) CONFLICT / non-compensatory pairs (trials 1, 2, 8, 10): the option favored by the single highest-validity discriminating cue is beaten on the tally (e.g. A=[1,0,0,0,0] vs B=[0,1,1,1,1], tally 1-4 for B). TTB predicts a confident choice of A; Tallying predicts a confident choice of B, with margin-graded confidence (4-cue margin in trials 1/8 vs 1-cue margin in trials 2/10).

(2) TALLY-TIE pairs (trials 3, 4): A wins two cues, B wins two cues, so Tallying is exactly at chance (50/50 regardless of beta and epsilon), whereas TTB decides confidently on the top cue. Any systematic deviation from 50% here is impossible for Tallying at any parameter setting and is therefore the sharpest single-trial discriminator.

(3) LOW-CUE-DECIDES pairs (trials 7, 9): the top two cues tie, the third cue (validity .75) discriminates in one direction while the two lowest cues both favor the other option, so TTB and Tallying make opposite predictions in a case where TTB has to descend the cascade rather than read the first cue.

(4) AGREEMENT pairs with different tally margins (trials 5, 6, 11, 12): both theories pick the same option, but Tallying's softmax makes accuracy strongly margin-dependent (4-1 vs 2-1), while TTB predicts identical choice probability sigmoid(beta) irrespective of margin. Comparing accuracy on trials 5/11 versus 6/12 gives a purely quantitative dissociation that does not depend on which option is 'correct'.

All pairs are mirrored across A and B to avoid side bias, and no pair is degenerate (every pair has at least one discriminating cue and the two theories either disagree in direction or in predicted confidence).

metric.rationale:
This is a within-subject, parameter-free contrast that isolates the one-reason signature of Take-The-Best while cancelling out each subject's overall noise level.

For every trial I recompute (a) the TTB winner (first discriminating cue in descending-validity feature order) and (b) the tally winner. Trials split into CONFLICT trials, where the two heuristics point to different options (design trials 1, 2, 7, 8, 9, 10), and AGREEMENT trials, where they point to the same option (trials 5, 6, 11, 12). Tally-tie pairs (3, 4) are dropped because they are uninformative for this particular contrast. The metric is P(choose the TTB-favoured option | conflict) minus P(choose the TTB-favoured option | agreement).

Predictions:
- Take-The-Best: choice probability for the top-cue winner is sigmoid(beta) softened by the lapse, identically on every decisive pair regardless of tally margin or conflict status. So the two rates are the same and the metric is exactly 0 in expectation, for ALL values of beta and epsilon. Only binomial sampling noise (48 vs 32 trials per class) contributes, giving a tight per-subject variance of roughly 0.013.
- Tallying: on conflict trials the subject systematically chooses AGAINST the TTB option (rate 1 - q), while on agreement trials they choose WITH it (rate q). The metric is therefore strongly negative, around -0.6 to -0.9 for any moderately decisive beta, with modest across-subject spread driven mostly by the lapse rate.

Because the TTB prediction is a hard zero that does not depend on the fitted nuisance parameters, and the Tallying prediction is a large negative number, the two theories should separate by roughly 0.7-0.8 with small per-subject variance on both sides. It is not trivially true for TTB in the sense of being a restatement of the model: any strategy that weights evidence compensatorily (tallying, weighted-additive, or even partial cue integration) will push the score negative, while pure one-reason decision making pins it at zero.

proposer_theory.description: People compare two options by consulting cues one at a time in order of validity, stopping at the first cue that discriminates between the two options. That cue alone determines the choice: the option with the higher value on the discriminating cue wins, and no other cue is consulted. Cues with lower validity are never reached when a higher-validity cue already discriminates, so Take The Best is a "one-reason" decision rule — only a single feature is ever used on any given choice. Because only the sign of the comparison on the top discriminating cue matters, TTB ignores both the magnitude of that difference and all information on lower-validity cues, making it maximally frugal in the use of evidence. Cue validities are subjective and can be learned, inferred from instructions, or fixed by task structure. When no cue discriminates (all feature-wise comparisons tie) the learner has no basis for preference and must guess. Response noise enters through a softmax over the binary TTB score (winner = 1, loser = 0) with inverse temperature beta, plus an independent lapse that with probability epsilon replaces the softmax output with a uniform pick over the two options.

def predict(parameters, stimulus, history):
    # Paper-faithful Take The Best (Gigerenzer & Goldstein 1996).
    # Stimulus is the pair of option feature vectors for the current
    # trial: array-like of shape (2, n_features), row 0 = option A,
    # row 1 = option B. Cue cascade: features are consulted in order
    # of descending validity; the first discriminating cue (strict
    # inequality) determines the winner; if no cue discriminates,
    # the model guesses uniformly. History is ignored.
    stim = np.asarray(stimulus, dtype=float)
    if stim.ndim != 2 or stim.shape[0] != 2:
        raise ValueError(
            f"TTB expects a (2, n_features) stimulus; got shape {stim.shape}."
        )
    n_features = stim.shape[1]

    val = np.asarray(parameters["validities"], dtype=float)
    if val.shape[0] != n_features:
        raise ValueError(
            f"validities length {val.shape[0]} != n_features {n_features}."
        )
    # Descending validity; argsort is stable so validity ties break
    # toward the earlier feature index.
    cue_order = np.argsort(-val, kind="stable").tolist()

    a, b = stim[0], stim[1]
    winner = None
    for j in cue_order:
        if a[j] > b[j]:
            winner = 0
            break
        if b[j] > a[j]:
            winner = 1
            break

    if winner is None:
        # No discriminating cue — pure guess.
        return np.ones(2) / 2.0

    scores = np.array([1.0, 0.0]) if winner == 0 else np.array([0.0, 1.0])

    beta = float(parameters["beta"])
    epsilon = float(parameters["epsilon"])

    # Softmax with max-subtraction for numerical stability. For the
    # binary TTB score this collapses to sigmoid(beta) for the winner,
    # giving a direct mapping from beta onto the paper's flip-noise
    # levels (beta=0 ↔ 50/50; beta ≫ 1 ↔ deterministic).
    z = beta * (scores - scores.max())
    e = np.exp(z)
    p_core = e / e.sum()

    n_opts = p_core.shape[0]
    return (1.0 - epsilon) * p_core + epsilon * (np.ones(n_opts) / n_opts)

experiment.rationale:
Six experts with well-spread but deliberately *non-monotone* validity order across screen positions (0.90, 0.60, 0.80, 0.55, 0.70, 0.95) so that Take-The-Best's cue cascade (f5 > f0 > f2 > f4 > f1 > f3) cannot be confused with a simple left-to-right reading strategy, while Tallying (which ignores order entirely) is unaffected. Twelve unique pairs, each repeated 8 times (96 trials), fall into four diagnostic classes.

(1) NON-COMPENSATORY CONFLICT with graded tally margin (trials 1-4). The single highest-validity cue (f5, 95%) favours one option while the tally favours the other, by margin 4 (trials 1, 2), margin 2 (trial 3) or margin 1 (trial 4). TTB predicts the SAME confidence sigmoid(beta) for all four, always siding with the f5 winner; Tallying predicts the opposite direction with confidence strictly increasing in the margin (sigmoid(4*beta) > sigmoid(2*beta) > sigmoid(beta)). Direction AND the margin gradient jointly identify the model.

(2) TALLY-TIE pairs (trials 5-8). Feature-wise wins are exactly balanced (3-3 in trials 5/6 with no ties; 2-2 with two tied cues in trials 7/8), so Tallying is pinned at exactly 50% for every (beta, epsilon) - no parameter setting can move it. TTB decides confidently: on trials 5/6 the top cue f5 discriminates immediately; on trials 7/8 f5 ties and TTB must descend to f0 (90%). Any systematic departure from chance here is impossible for Tallying, making these the sharpest single-cell discriminators, and trials 7/8 additionally verify that subjects use validity rank rather than screen position.

(3) LOW-CUE-DECIDES CONFLICT (trials 9, 10). The two most valid cues (f5, f0) tie; the third-ranked cue f2 (80%) discriminates one way while the three lower cues (f4, f1, f3) all favour the other option (tally 1-3). TTB must walk the cascade and then choose against the majority; Tallying chooses the majority. Opposite directions in a case where TTB's one-reason logic is hardest to mimic.

(4) AGREEMENT pairs with extreme margin contrast (trials 11, 12). Both theories favour the same option, but with tally margin 5 (trial 11) versus margin 1 (trial 12). TTB predicts identical accuracy on the two; Tallying predicts near-ceiling on trial 11 and markedly lower accuracy on trial 12. This is a purely quantitative dissociation that is independent of choice direction and of any objective 'correct' answer.

All classes are mirrored across sides (TTB predicts A on 6 pairs and B on 6; Tallying's non-tie predictions are likewise 4/4), so side bias cannot masquerade as either model. No pair is degenerate: every pair has at least one discriminating cue, and in every pair the two theories differ either in predicted direction or in predicted confidence.

metric.rationale: The design contains pairs where the highest-validity cue (f5, or f2 after f5/f0 tie) points one way while the feature tally points the other way with a margin of at least 2 (trials 1, 2, 3, 9, 10). Restricting to margin>=2 conflicts guarantees that Tallying is confident (softmax on a tally difference of 2-4 saturates for almost all beta in the allowed range), so Tallying predicts choice of the tally winner at rate (1-eps)*sigmoid(margin*beta)+eps/2, typically ~0.85-1.0. Take-The-Best predicts exactly the opposite option at rate (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta)+eps/2, so its tally-consistency rate is typically ~0.0-0.15. The metric is a simple proportion over 40 pooled trials per subject, so binomial noise is small, and the only between-subject spread comes from the lapse parameter eps (bounded contribution <= 0.25). This yields a mean gap of roughly 0.7-0.75 with per-subject variance on the order of 0.01, which is far beyond what N=25 needs. It is not trivially true for Tallying: it is a directional prediction on genuinely conflicting evidence, and any subject who consults more than one reason but weights cues (e.g., weighted-additive) would also land high, while a strict one-reason decider lands low.

proposer_theory.description: People compare two options by counting, across all features, how often one option has a higher value than the other. The option that wins on more features is chosen. Tallying discards cardinal magnitudes — only the sign of each feature-wise comparison matters — so the heuristic is robust to monotone rescaling of individual features and cannot be swayed by a single large feature difference in the way Equal-Weight can. Ties on an individual feature contribute nothing to either count: that cue is simply treated as uninformative for the pair. No feature is privileged, in contrast to Take The Best; every cue contributes equally to the tally. When the two counts are equal the heuristic has no basis for preference and the learner must guess. Response noise enters through a softmax over the two tallies with inverse temperature beta (interpolating between fully deterministic choice at large beta and uniform guessing at beta = 0), plus an independent lapse that with probability epsilon replaces the softmax output with a uniform pick over the two options.

def predict(parameters, stimulus, history):
    # Paper-faithful Tallying heuristic (Dawes 1979; Gigerenzer &
    # Goldstein 1999). Stimulus is the pair of option feature vectors
    # for the current trial: array-like of shape (2, n_features),
    # with row 0 = option A, row 1 = option B. History is ignored.
    stim = np.asarray(stimulus, dtype=float)
    if stim.ndim != 2 or stim.shape[0] != 2:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Tallying expects a (2, n_features) stimulus; got shape {stim.shape}."
        )

    a, b = stim[0], stim[1]
    # Count strict feature-wise wins; ties contribute to neither option.
    a_wins = float(np.sum(a > b))
    b_wins = float(np.sum(b > a))
    scores = np.array([a_wins, b_wins])

    beta = float(parameters["beta"])
    epsilon = float(parameters["epsilon"])

    # Softmax with max-subtraction for numerical stability. When
    # a_wins == b_wins the softmax is exactly uniform regardless of
    # beta, which is the correct behavior for an undiscriminating
    # tally.
    z = beta * (scores - scores.max())
    e = np.exp(z)
    p_core = e / e.sum()

    n_opts = p_core.shape[0]
    return (1.0 - epsilon) * p_core + epsilon * (np.ones(n_opts) / n_opts)

next_theory.description:
**Serial-position–driven, primacy/recency-graded evidence accumulation ("read-order scanning").**

People do not re-sort the expert ratings by the stated validities before deciding. They inspect the ratings in the order in which they appear on the screen (reading order) and their attention decays sharply across that inspection sequence, so the evidence carried by a cue is discounted geometrically by its *serial position*, not by its validity. Stated validities exert only a weak, partial pull on the inspection order (parameter gamma, small).

Two further claims:

1. **The gradient is steep but graded.** Weights fall off as w_j = exp(-lambda * rank_j) with |lambda| well above zero, so decisions are usually driven by the first cue(s) that discriminate — near-lexicographic but not strictly all-or-none: when the leading cues tie, the next-inspected cues take over, and when several later cues line up they can occasionally overturn a leading cue if the gradient is shallow.

2. **The gradient has a sign: most readers are primacy-oriented, a substantial minority are recency-oriented.** Reading a short list produces either an anchoring-on-the-first-item strategy (primacy, lambda > 0) or a last-impression-counts strategy (recency, lambda < 0). The population is bimodal: about one third of subjects anchor on the *last-read* cue. Near-zero gradients (i.e., genuine equal-weight tallying) are essentially absent — people do not integrate all six/five cues equally.

Evidence is evaluated *relatively*: the signed weighted difference is normalised by the total weight of the cues that actually discriminate, so a decision based on one early cue is as confident as a decision based on many, and only genuinely near-balanced weighted evidence produces hesitation. Choice is a softmax on this relative evidence with inverse temperature beta, plus a lapse epsilon.

Because validity order and screen order coincide in a validity-sorted display but dissociate in a scrambled display, this theory predicts TTB-looking behaviour in the former and tally-looking behaviour in the latter — without either heuristic being the actual mechanism. The causal driver is *where the cue sits on the screen*.
next_theory.predict_source:
def predict(parameters, state, history):
    import numpy as np

    # ---- unpack the trial stimulus -> (2, n_features) ------------------
    if isinstance(state, dict):
        a = np.asarray(list(state.get('option_a_ratings', [])), dtype=float)
        b = np.asarray(list(state.get('option_b_ratings', [])), dtype=float)
        stim = np.vstack([a, b])
    else:
        stim = np.asarray(state, dtype=float)
        if stim.ndim == 1:
            stim = stim.reshape(2, -1)
        elif stim.ndim > 2:
            stim = stim.reshape(2, -1)
    if stim.shape[0] != 2:
        stim = stim.reshape(2, -1)

    a = stim[0].astype(float)
    b = stim[1].astype(float)
    n = a.shape[0]
    d = a - b

    # ---- inspection ranks: screen position, weakly pulled by validity --
    val = parameters.get('validities', None)
    try:
        val = np.asarray(val, dtype=float).ravel()
    except Exception:
        val = None
    if val is None or val.shape[0] != n:
        # fallback: assume the display is already validity-sorted
        val = np.linspace(0.95, 0.55, n)

    order = np.argsort(-val, kind='stable')       # 0 = highest validity
    vrank = np.empty(n, dtype=float)
    vrank[order] = np.arange(n, dtype=float)
    pos = np.arange(n, dtype=float)               # reading-order index

    gamma = float(parameters.get('gamma', 0.0))
    gamma = min(max(gamma, 0.0), 1.0)
    rank = gamma * vrank + (1.0 - gamma) * pos

    # ---- signed attention gradient (primacy vs recency reader) --------
    lam_mag = float(parameters.get('lam', 2.0))
    orient = float(parameters.get('scan_orientation', 1.0))
    RECENCY_SHARE = 0.35                          # population constant
    lam = -lam_mag if orient < RECENCY_SHARE else lam_mag

    z = -lam * (rank - float(np.mean(rank)))      # centered for stability
    z = z - float(np.max(z))
    w = np.exp(z)

    # ---- relative (normalised) weighted evidence ----------------------
    num = float(np.sum(w * d))
    den = float(np.sum(w * np.abs(d)))
    if den <= 1e-12:
        S = 0.0                                   # nothing discriminates
    else:
        S = num / den                             # in [-1, 1]

    beta = float(parameters.get('beta', 6.0))
    eps = float(parameters.get('epsilon', 0.0))
    eps = min(max(eps, 0.0), 1.0)

    logits = np.array([beta * S, 0.0], dtype=float)
    logits = logits - np.max(logits)
    e = np.exp(logits)
    p = e / np.sum(e)

    p = (1.0 - eps) * p + eps * 0.5
    p = np.clip(p, 1e-12, 1.0)
    p = p / p.sum()
    return p
next_theory.rationale:
**Why the incumbents fail.** pi_1 (validity-ordered TTB) reproduces Experiment 1 (metric ~0) but collapses in Experiment 2 (0.15 vs 0.775), because in Exp 2 the validities are scrambled relative to screen position and TTB's top cue (position 5, validity .95) systematically opposes the tally. pi_2 (Tallying) does the reverse (0.87 in Exp 2, -0.69 in Exp 1). Neither is experiment-invariant, and the key structural difference between the two experiments is precisely that Exp 1's display is validity-sorted while Exp 2's is not. That is the arbiter's diagnosis and it is exactly right: *screen position*, not validity, is the causal variable.

**What this model does mechanistically.** Weights decay geometrically along the inspection sequence, which is essentially the reading order (gamma <= 0.25 gives validities only a weak pull). In Exp 1 position order = validity order, so a primacy reader looks TTB-like (metric ~0). In Exp 2 a primacy reader always uses position 0 first; I verified by hand that on every one of the five qualifying conflict trials in Exp 2 (rows 1, 2, 3, 9, 10) the first *positionally* discriminating cue points at the **tally** winner, so primacy readers score ~1.0 there — i.e. they mimic Tallying without counting anything.

**Why the signed gradient (the novel ingredient).** A purely primacy model predicts exactly 0.0 in Exp 1, whereas humans are slightly *above* 0 (+0.093): they are marginally more TTB-consistent on conflict than on agree trials. No decay-only or one-reason model can produce a positive value; graded integration makes it negative. A recency-oriented reader (lambda < 0, anchoring on the last-read cue) yields exactly the required asymmetry: I computed that such a subject scores 1/3 on Exp-1 conflict trials but 0 on Exp-1 agree trials (metric = +1/3), and 0.4 on Exp-2 conflict trials. Mixing ~35% recency readers with ~65% primacy readers therefore predicts Exp 1 ~ +0.08 to +0.09 and Exp 2 ~ 0.76 to 0.78, hitting both observed values (0.093, 0.775) simultaneously — something no single-strategy model in the leaderboard can do. The bimodality claim (|lambda| bounded away from 0) is substantive: it asserts that true equal-weight integration is rare, which is what rules out the pi_2-style -0.69 in Exp 1.

**Relative-evidence normalisation.** Dividing the signed weighted sum by the total weight of discriminating cues means a decision resting on a single early cue is held with the same confidence as one resting on many, so trials whose leading cues tie (e.g. Exp 1 rows 7/9) do not degenerate into coin flips under a steep gradient. This keeps error rates roughly uniform across trial types and prevents the spurious negative bias that a raw-magnitude softmax would inject into the Exp-1 metric.

**Nesting and falsifiability.** lambda -> 0 recovers Tallying, lambda -> +inf with gamma -> 1 recovers TTB, gamma -> 0 gives pure reading-order scanning, and the sign of lambda captures primacy vs recency. The theory makes the sharp, testable prediction the arbiter asked for: scrambling the on-screen order of the same experts while holding the pair structure fixed should reverse choices on top-cue-vs-tally conflict pairs, whereas validity-based accounts predict invariance.

experiment.rationale:
GOAL: dissociate Take-The-Best (validity-ordered lexicographic search) from the 'read-order scanning' model (geometric weighting by SCREEN position, primacy for ~65% of subjects, recency for ~35%, with only a weak validity pull gamma<=0.25).

KEY DESIGN MOVE: the display order is deliberately NOT validity-ordered, and crucially the top-validity cue is placed in the MIDDLE of the screen (position 3, 95%), while the second-best cue sits at the END (position 5, 85%) and a mid-validity cue sits FIRST (position 0, 70%). Validities by screen position are [.70, .55, .60, .95, .65, .85], so TTB's cue cascade is pos3 > pos5 > pos0 > pos4 > pos2 > pos1. A primacy scanner anchors on pos0, a recency scanner anchors on pos5, and TTB anchors on pos3 -- three mutually distinguishable anchors. I verified numerically that this ordering is robust across the scanning model's whole parameter range: even at the maximum validity pull (gamma=.25) and the shallowest gradient (lam=1.2), pos0 still has the largest primacy weight and pos5 the largest recency weight, so the predictions below do not depend on lucky parameter values. (This is why pos0 was given 0.70 rather than the lowest validity: with a low-validity first cue the gamma=.25 pull would have flipped the primacy anchor onto the top-validity cue and destroyed the dissociation.)

TRIAL CLASSES (12 unique pairs, each repeated 8x = 96 trials; every pair mirrored across sides so side bias cannot mimic either model; TTB predicts A on 6 and B on 6, and so do both scanning orientations).

(1) DOUBLE-DISSOCIATION pairs 1-2 (A=[1,0,0,0,0,1] vs B=[0,0,0,1,0,0] and mirror). Only pos0, pos3, pos5 discriminate; the two screen-EXTREME cues favour one option and the top-validity MIDDLE cue favours the other. TTB must choose the pos3 option; BOTH primacy and recency scanners choose the other option (checked numerically for lam in [1.2,3.5] x gamma in [0,.25]: |S|>0.78 in every case). These are the sharpest cells -- no setting of the scanning model's parameters, of either orientation, can reproduce TTB here.

(2) PRIMACY-vs-TTB pairs 3-4 and 7-8. Pair 3: pos0 favours A, pos3 favours B, nothing else discriminates -> TTB=B, recency=B, primacy=A. Pair 7: pos3 ties so TTB must DESCEND to pos5 (A) while pos0 favours B -> TTB=A, recency=A, primacy=B. These isolate primacy readers and simultaneously verify that subjects use validity rank, not left-to-right position, when the leading screen cue conflicts with the cascade.

(3) RECENCY-vs-TTB pairs 5-6. pos3 (95%) favours B, pos5 (85%) favours A, nothing else discriminates -> TTB=B, primacy=B, recency=A. These isolate recency readers.

(4) COMPENSATORY / GRADED-CONFIDENCE pairs 9-12. Pair 9 (A=[1,0,0,0,0,0] vs B=[0,1,1,0,0,0]): one early cue against two slightly later, lower-validity cues -> TTB=A confidently, primacy=A but with markedly reduced relative evidence (S ~= 0.44-0.59 depending on lam), recency=B. Pair 11 (A=[0,0,0,0,0,1] vs B=[1,1,1,0,0,0]): the single last-position 85% cue against the three leading cues -> TTB=A, recency=A (S ~= 0.57-1.0), primacy=B with near-maximal evidence. Because TTB's choice probability is the SAME sigmoid(beta) on every non-tied pair, any systematic accuracy gradient across pairs 3/7 (near-|S|=1 for the scanner) versus pairs 9/11 (intermediate |S|) is a purely quantitative signature of the scanning model that TTB cannot produce at any (beta, epsilon).

DIAGNOSTIC YIELD: for a primacy subject TTB and the scanning model disagree in DIRECTION on 8 of 12 pairs (1,2,3,4,7,8,11,12); for a recency subject they disagree on 6 of 12 (1,2,5,6,9,10). Under TTB, choices should track pos3 (then pos5) regardless of screen position; under the competitor, choices should track pos0 (or pos5) and show margin-graded confidence. Every pair has at least one discriminating cue, so no cell is degenerate.

metric.rationale: Take-The-Best must decide these trials on the single top-validity cue, which sits at screen position 3 (validity .95). On trial pairs 1-2 the two screen-EXTREME cues (position 0 = .70 and position 5 = .85) favour the option that the top-validity middle cue opposes. TTB therefore chooses the position-3 option on essentially every such trial (rate = (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta)+eps/2, expected ~0.85 across the parameter range, and never below 0.5). The read-order scanning model, by contrast, chooses the OPPOSITE option under BOTH orientations: a primacy reader anchors on position 0 (rank 0, weight ratio > e^2.1 over position 3 even at maximum validity pull gamma=.25), and a recency reader anchors on position 5 (highest rank). So the scanner's rate is ~eps/2 + sigmoid noise, i.e. ~0.03, and crucially it is the SAME (~0.03) for primacy and recency subjects, so the population mixture does not inflate between-subject variance. The metric selects these trials structurally (top cue discriminates, positions 0 and 5 both discriminate in the opposite direction) rather than by hard-coded trial index, works identically on pooled and single-subject data, and yields a mean gap of roughly 0.82 with small per-subject variance on both sides.

    # trial: array-like of shape (2, n_features), row 0 = option A,
    # row 1 = option B. Cue cascade: features are consulted in order
    # of descending validity; the first discriminating cue (strict
    # inequality) determines the winner; if no cue discriminates,
    # the model guesses uniformly. History is ignored.
    stim = np.asarray(stimulus, dtype=float)
    if stim.ndim != 2 or stim.shape[0] != 2:
        raise ValueError(
            f"TTB expects a (2, n_features) stimulus; got shape {stim.shape}."
        )
    n_features = stim.shape[1]

    val = np.asarray(parameters["validities"], dtype=float)
    if val.shape[0] != n_features:
        raise ValueError(
            f"validities length {val.shape[0]} != n_features {n_features}."
        )
